title: The puzzle of hot water freezing
text: {{1}} hot water can freeze faster {{2}} cold water is a question that has divided natural philosophers since Aristotle. The modern chapter began in 1963, when Erasto Mpemba, {{3}} was then a Tanzanian schoolboy, noticed that his hot ice-cream mixture froze solid before his classmates' cooler batches had set. Not until 1969 {{4}} a physics paper take his observation seriously, and the phenomenon {{5}} duly named the Mpemba effect. It remains {{6}} be fully explained: candidates include evaporation, convection currents and dissolved gases, yet laboratory results stubbornly refuse to agree, and scientists still argue over {{7}} it happens at all. There is {{8}} single agreed explanation, and the effect may yet disappear under stricter scrutiny — a humbling reminder that even kitchen physics can keep secrets.

gaps.hint: conjunction: ___ hot water can freeze faster
gaps.explanation: Fronted subject clause presenting the open question; 'if' cannot begin a subject clause.

gaps.hint: relative: Mpemba, ___ was then a schoolboy
gaps.explanation: Non-defining relative referring to a person after the comma.

gaps.hint: auxiliary: not until 1969 ___ a paper take
gaps.explanation: Inversion after 'not until': the auxiliary 'did' carries the past tense.
Past passive with a singular subject: it was named.
'Remains to be explained' — the infinitive after 'remains'.

gaps.hint: question word: argue over ___ it happens
gaps.explanation: The reason is disputed: argue over why.

gaps.hint: determiner: there is ___ single agreed explanation
gaps.explanation: 'No' negates the noun phrase; 'not' cannot stand before 'single'.
